title: Cloud Persistence
overview: Choose persistence from the data shape, access pattern, consistency requirement and scale. Trace relational and object databases into the four NoSQL families, then compare sharding, replication and eventual consistency. Map local, file, block, object and database storage to cloud services while accounting for the operating cost of multiple stores.
big_ideas: Relational stores support integrity, joins and ACID transactions; distributing those guarantees has coordination costs.
Big data (the six V's: Volume, Velocity, Variety, Variability, Veracity, Value) pushed web giants to build NoSQL stores.
NoSQL is best read as **Not Only SQL**: a family of key-value, column-family, document and graph stores, each suited to a different data shape and access pattern.
**Polyglot persistence**: use the right storage technology for each use case, but weigh the gain against the extra programming and operational complexity.
Sharding divides records among nodes; replication copies records for availability or reads. Multi-writer replicas add coordination and conflict-handling work.
Some distributed workloads favour BASE and eventual consistency; distribution does not make ACID impossible.
Cloud storage: ephemeral instance disk, shared network files, persistent block volumes and API-accessed objects; check lifecycle and access semantics.
AWS examples: RDS/Aurora for relational transactions, DynamoDB for key-value/documents, Redshift for analytical columnar storage, ElastiCache for caching and Neptune for graphs.

sections.title: Why persistence matters in the cloud
sections.summary: The basic question: can traditional data storage keep up as applications move from a single server and database to distributed cloud deployments?

notes.h: Data distribution is an explicit choice
notes.lead: Cloud deployment makes data distribution an explicit design choice.
items: **Multiple application instances** may **share one database** or use **several stores and regions**
**Not every cloud app needs many databases**
Evolves with the **nature of the data**
Recurring question → do **current designs still meet evolving needs**?

terms.def: Storing data so it survives beyond the process or request that created it.

check.q: An app moves from one server to 6 load-balanced instances in the cloud, and users start losing their shopping carts between requests. What changed in the persistence problem?

items: **One server**: each instance kept **cart state locally** → worked
**6 load-balanced instances**: requests land on **different instances** → local state fails, carts lost
**Distributed deployment** → you must decide which state is **shared**, **where it lives** and how it **survives an instance failure**
**Fix**: move carts to a **shared store**
a.foot: **Cost**: a **network call per request** + a **new component** that must be available.

check.q: A team starting a new cloud app with modest load plans four different databases from day one 'because that's cloud-native'. Do you agree?

items: **Cloud deployment** makes **data distribution** an **explicit choice**, not a requirement to use many stores
**Start simple**: a single **managed relational database** may be enough at first
**Add** stores, **partitioning** or **replication** when **access patterns**, **scale** or **availability requirements** justify it

sections.title: Database history: navigational, relational, object
sections.summary: Database generations: hierarchical and network (1960s), relational with normalisation and ACID (1970s), and object databases (1990s), ending with RDBMS strengths and its scaling weakness.

notes.h: Each database generation fixed a pain
items: **Hierarchical model** (1960s) → **tree**, **one parent per child** (e.g. **IMS**)
**Network model** (1960s) → **graph**, **many parents** (e.g. **IDMS**)
Both **tied access to the physical structure**
**Relational model** (1970s, **Codd**) → describes how data is **presented, not stored**; **tables joined on keys**
notes.foot: Each generation fixed the **previous one's pain**.

items.t: **Normalisation** → split data into **smaller tables joined at query time** to:

items: Behind **one uniform (declarative) language**: **SQL**
Tried to remove the **object-relational mismatch**
**Stored objects directly** → **identity**, **inheritance**, **no normalisation**
**Failed to win market share**
**ORM tools** solved much of the mismatch on top of **mature RDBMS** instead
ORM example → **flattening an inheritance hierarchy** into **one table with a type column**
**Mature and precise** (**star schemas**, **reporting**)
But **expensive to scale**

terms.def: Tree-structured database where each child record has exactly one parent (e.g. IBM IMS).
Graph-structured database where records can have many parents and children (e.g. IDMS).
Splitting data into smaller related tables to remove duplication and update anomalies.
Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability: guarantees of a reliable transaction.
Object-oriented database that stores program objects directly, without normalising them.
Object-Relational Mapping: a layer that maps program objects to relational tables.

check.q: A legacy hierarchical database makes a new 'all orders for product X across customers' report very slow, because data is reached from customer records down. Why does the relational model help here?

items: **Navigational models** tie access to the **physical tree** → a query that doesn't follow the **parent-child path** has to **traverse everything**
**Relational model** separates how data is **presented** from how it is **stored**
→ the same **normalised tables** can be **joined** in whatever **direction** a new query needs

check.q: A team wants an object database because 'mapping our class hierarchy to tables is painful'. What does history suggest, and what would you propose?

a.lead: **Propose an ORM over a relational database**, or a **document store** if the objects really are **self-contained aggregates**.
items: **History**: **object databases** did address the **object-relational mismatch**, but never won **market share**
**ORM tools** solved much of the mismatch on top of **mature relational databases**
**Example**: flatten an **inheritance hierarchy** into **one table** with a **type column**

check.q: A finance system needs precise reporting, star schemas and strict integrity, and is expected to grow tenfold in 5 years. Is a relational database still a sound choice?

items: **Mature and precise**: **normalisation**, **ACID**, **SQL** for reporting
**Risk**: its main weakness → **expensive to scale** for very large **distributed workloads**
**Plan for that growth**: **bigger instances**, **read replicas**, **partitioning**, or **NewSQL** later
a.foot: Plan for growth rather than **giving up integrity** now.

sections.title: Big data and the birth of NoSQL
sections.summary: How the six V's exposed RDBMS limits, how Google, Amazon, Facebook and others built their own stores, how NoSQL got its name, the three kinds of data structure, and polyglot persistence.

notes.h: Big data (six V's) exposed RDBMS limits
items: **Volume** → **scale-out** on **commodity/cloud**, not **one big server**
**Velocity** → **real-time performance** via **distributed persistence**
**Variety** → **non-static schemas** for **structured, semi-structured, unstructured** data
**Variability** → **agility**: **always-on services**, **frequent releases**
**Veracity** → **trustworthiness**
**Value** → **turning data into value**
Lecture's **keyword-to-URL** example → needs **huge distributed lookups**, not **complex joins** and **multi-record transactions**
**Bigtable** belongs to the **column-family lineage**
**Large volume across servers**
**Low latency**
**Very high availability**
**Incremental scaling** with **no downtime**
**Tolerance of network partitions**
**Cheap commodity hardware** without **lock-in**
**Several non-relational data models**, not **one guarantee set**
**Structured** data → has an **explicit model**
**Semi-structured** (e.g. **JSON/XML**) → **flexible structure**
**Unstructured** text or media → may need **search, extraction or ML** depending on the task
**Different storage technologies** for **different needs**
Applies **across an enterprise** or **within one application**
**Wrap data access in services** → **limit the impact** of each choice
Every extra technology adds **programming and operational complexity**

terms.def: Volume, Velocity, Variety, Variability, Veracity, Value: the characteristics of big data.
'Not Only SQL': a family of non-relational databases (key-value, column, document, graph).
Data with a flexible schema such as JSON or XML.
Using multiple storage technologies, each chosen for how a particular component uses its data.
Adding more commodity servers rather than buying a bigger single server (scale-up).

check.q: Using the search example from the lecture, explain why a relational database was a poor fit for a keyword-to-URL lookup at web scale.

items: **Workload**: a huge, **read-mostly lookup** spread across **many servers**
**No need** for **multi-record transactions**, many **entities** or **integrity constraints**
**Relational database** → provides **features the workload doesn't use** + makes the **distribution** it does need **costly**
a.foot: Where **joins and transactions** matter, the **balance reverses**.

check.q: An IoT platform ingests 50,000 sensor readings a second, and each device type sends a different set of fields. Which of the V's are causing pressure, and what do they point to?

a.lead: **Velocity, Volume, Variety** together point to a **distributed NoSQL store** for the **raw readings**.
items: **Velocity**: **real-time ingestion** needs **distributed persistence** for **throughput**
**Volume**: **scale out** on **commodity or cloud servers**, not one big server
**Variety**: fields differ by device → a **non-static schema** helps
a.foot: Keep any **transactional data**, such as **billing**, wherever its **integrity needs** are best met.

check.q: A 5-person team proposes a graph database, a document store, a cache and a relational database for an app with 2,000 users. When is polyglot persistence a bad idea, and what would you do?

a.lead: **Bad idea when** the **gain** from a better **storage fit** is smaller than the **cost of programming and operating** each extra technology, likely here given the **team size** and **load**.
items: **Start with fewer stores**
**Add one** only when an **access pattern** clearly needs it
**Wrap data access in services** → a later change has **limited impact**

sections.title: The four NoSQL data store patterns
sections.summary: The four NoSQL patterns (key-value, column family, document, graph): what each stores and typical uses.

notes.h: Four NoSQL patterns: unit of storage
items: **Key-value** → a **value looked up by a single key** (caches, lookup tables, file stores)
**Column family** → **sparse data keyed by row and column**, columns **grouped into families read together** (web crawling, large sparse tables)
**Document** → a whole **tree-structured object in one unit** (orders, invoices, forms, web pages)
**Graph** → **nodes, edges and properties** (social, **friend-of-friend**, **pattern matching**)
Group related **object data**
An **order and its line items** read as **one aggregate**, without **reconstructing normalised tables**
**Simplifies object-shaped reads**
**Cross-document relationships and constraints** still need **deliberate modelling**
**Row-oriented** → each **row an aggregate** (e.g. **customer 1234**, with families like **profile** and **order history**)
**Column-oriented** → each **family a record type**; a **row** is the **join across families**
**Nodes and edges** express **relationship-heavy questions**
Example → **friend-of-friend recommendations**
Advantage depends on the **traversal workload**, **indexes** and **dataset**
**Not universally faster than joins**

terms.def: Database that maps a unique key to a value, like a distributed dictionary or hash.
A named group of columns stored and accessed together under a row key.
Database that stores a self-contained document (e.g. JSON) per object.
Database that stores nodes and edges with properties for relationship traversal.

check.q: Invoices are always read and written as a whole, with header and line items together, and the format varies by country. Document store or normalised relational tables?

items: **Natural aggregate**: each invoice **maps to one document** → reads need **no joins**
**Varying fields** → no **schema changes** needed
a.foot: **Give up**: easy **cross-invoice constraints** and **ad-hoc joins** (e.g. **reporting across customers and products**) → may need a separate **reporting store**.

check.q: A social app's 'people you may know' query joins the friendships table to itself three levels deep and is slow. Which pattern fits, and what should you check before switching?

a.lead: **A graph store**: the question is **relationship traversal** across **nodes and edges**, rather than **repeated joins**.
items: **Check** that the real workload is **traversal-heavy**
**Benchmark** it with **realistic data** and **indexes** → graph stores are **not universally faster** than joins
**Keep other data**, such as **profiles**, in whatever store suits it

check.q: In a column-family store, customer rows have a profile family and an order-history family. A screen reads only the profile. Why does the grouping matter?

items: **Column family**: columns assumed to be **read together** are **stored together** → reading the profile doesn't pull the large **order history**
**Sparse rows**: customers **without orders cost nothing**
**Choose families from the access patterns**
a.foot: A screen that needs **both families in one read** loses this benefit.

items.label: Key-value
items.detail: Dictionary, image store, document/file store, query cache, lookup tables.

items.label: Column family
items.detail: Web crawling, large sparsely populated tables, highly adaptable systems. Columns grouped in families accessed together.

items.label: Document
items.detail: Sales orders, invoices, product descriptions, forms, web pages. Object model turns directly into a document.

items.label: Graph
items.detail: Social network and friend-of-friends queries, inference, rules systems, pattern matching.

sections.title: Choosing a store: KV, column, document, graph, NewSQL
sections.summary: Decision criteria and product examples for each NoSQL type, ending with a SQL vs NoSQL vs NewSQL comparison.

items: **Key-value** → **direct keyed reads**, **caching**, suitable **specialised structures** (e.g. **Redis rankings**)
**Column-family** → **large sparse records** organised by **row key and families**
**Documents** → **flexible nested aggregates**
**Graphs** → **relationship traversal**
notes.foot: **Data size alone does not decide** the family; **model the queries and update patterns**.

notes.h: Check guarantees at the operation's scope
items: **Relational** → natural fit for **joins, constraints and ACID transactions**
**NoSQL** → capabilities **vary by product and operation**; **some offer transactions**
**NewSQL** → aims to combine **relational/SQL semantics** with **distributed scale**; **coordination costs** to evaluate

notes.lead: Read the lecture's comparison table as a simplification.
items: **Traditional relational** systems can be **costly to scale out**
That does **not** mean SQL is **inherently slow** or **unable to distribute**
**NoSQL does not universally exclude** **schemas**, **SQL-like queries** or **ACID**
A **column-family store** ≠ an **analytical columnar warehouse** such as **Redshift**
Derive **data elements** and a **schema** for a **shopping-cart page**
→ applying these choices to a **concrete scenario**

terms.def: Replicas may differ briefly but converge to the same value once updates stop.
Data must fit a defined schema when written (typical of RDBMS).
Relational, SQL and ACID databases that also scale horizontally like NoSQL.

check.q: A game needs a real-time global leaderboard updated thousands of times a second. Which store type fits, and what would you keep elsewhere?

a.lead: **An in-memory key-value store** with **sorted structures** such as **rankings**.
items: **Why**: a leaderboard is **direct keyed access** that must be **very fast**
**Keep elsewhere**: **durable data** such as **player accounts** and **purchases** → a **durable store**
a.foot: A **cache can lose data on failure** unless **persistence is configured**.

check.q: A team picks a column-family store because 'we'll have terabytes of data'. Is size a good reason, and what should decide it?

a.lead: **No. Data size alone** doesn't decide the **store family**.

sub: **Column-family**: **row-key access** to large **sparse records** grouped into families

items: **Model the access patterns**, then **benchmark the real queries**

check.q: A payments company needs SQL, strong ACID transactions and horizontal scale across regions. Is NewSQL the obvious answer?

items: **NewSQL** aims to combine **relational and SQL semantics** with **distributed scale**
**Evaluate the coordination cost**: **distributed guarantees** add **latency**, especially **across regions**
**Compare** with a **sharded relational design** and with **NoSQL products** that offer **transactions** at the **scope** you need

check.q: An analyst asks to run sales reports on the operational column-family store 'because both are columnar, like the warehouse'. What is the misunderstanding?

items: **Column-family store**: groups **sparse, row-keyed records** for **operational access**
**Analytical columnar warehouse**: a **SQL store** built for **large scans** and **aggregations**
**Heavy reports** on the operational store → **perform poorly** + **compete with live traffic**

visuals.title: Database families: tendencies, not guarantees
visuals.caption: Select by workload and required guarantees; no database label guarantees high performance.

sections.title: Sharding, replication and eventual consistency
sections.summary: The two ways to distribute data (sharding and replication), the two replication styles, and why distributed stores often settle for BASE instead of ACID.

sub: each serves **reads and writes for its subset**
e.g. **Singapore orders** on a Singapore node, **Malaysia orders** on a Malaysia node

items.t: **Replication** → **copies the same data** to several servers:

items: **Single-leader (master-slave)** → writes to **one leader**; may serve **reads from followers**; **failover must be designed**
**Peer-to-peer** → **multiple writers**; **conflict resolution** and **replication overhead** matter
**More writers** do not guarantee **linear write throughput**
When **stale reads are acceptable** → **asynchronous propagation** can favour **availability** and **lower coordination**

sub: **Eventually consistent** → copies **converge once updates stop and propagation completes**

items: **Distributed ACID remains possible** when its **coordination cost is justified**
**Keep ACID** → **money-critical** data
**Accept eventual consistency** → where **availability and scale** matter more than **instant agreement**

terms.def: Horizontal partitioning: different subsets of data stored on different servers.
Keeping copies of the same data on multiple servers.
One node accepts writes and copies them to slaves that may serve reads.
Any node accepts writes and nodes synchronise with each other.
Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency: the relaxed alternative to ACID.

check.q: An app is overwhelmed by writes. A teammate proposes adding read replicas with master-slave replication. Will it help? What would?

items: **Replicas** add **read capacity**, but **every write** still goes to the **single leader** → **write bottleneck stays**
**Shard** by a suitable key → **independent writes** go to **different servers**
**Peer-to-peer replication** may help some workloads, but each update still has to **propagate** and may need **conflict handling**

check.q: A regional retailer stores Singapore and Malaysia orders together and has one global product list. How would you distribute each kind of data?

items: **Orders** → **shard by country**: each node handles its **own reads and writes**, spreading both **volume** and **write load**
**Product list** → **replicate to every node**: **read-heavy** and **shared**; **single-leader replication** fits since **writes are rare**
a.foot: **Trade-off**: **cross-country reports** now need to **query several shards**.

check.q: A bank's product team wants eventual consistency 'everywhere, for scale'. Where would you allow it and where not?

items: **ACID (transactional)**: **authoritative balances** and **transfers** → **temporarily inconsistent** balances are **wrong and costly**
**Eventual consistency (BASE)**: **derived views** such as an **activity feed**, **analytics** or a **product listing** → a **briefly stale read** does little harm
a.foot: State the **consistency requirement per operation** instead of setting **one policy** for the whole system.

check.q: After switching to peer-to-peer replication, two regions accept conflicting updates to the same customer record during a network split. What caused this, and what are the options?

items: **Cause**: **multiple writers** + **asynchronous propagation** favour **availability** → both regions **accepted writes** and the **copies diverged**

sub: **Home region**: route each record's writes to it
**Coordinated writes** for that data → cost **latency** and **availability during a split**

visuals.title: Sharding vs replication
rows: Data volume; both reads and writes
Read capacity and availability; multi-writer throughput depends on coordination

sections.title: Cloud persistence options: file storage types
sections.summary: The cloud persistence options (files and databases) and the four file storage types with durability, sharing, analogies and AWS examples.

items: **Instance-store disk** → **ephemeral**; suits **scratch data**
**EFS** → **shared file access**
**EBS** → **persistent block storage**, normally a **disk for an attached VM**; **retention settings** decide whether it **survives VM deletion**
**S3** → stores **objects through APIs**, not a normal **mounted filesystem**
**Temporary scratch** → **local disk**
**Shared files across instances** → **network file system**
**Fast durable disk for one VM** (e.g. **database files**) → **mounted volume**
**Data used by many apps and channels** → **object storage**: the **most flexible and ubiquitous** option

terms.def: Storage exposed as disk blocks to an attached VM; concurrent sharing requires explicit storage and filesystem support.
Storage of files plus metadata accessed over a REST API (e.g. S3).
Instance-local disk whose data is lost when the instance stops or terminates.

check.q: A load-balanced web fleet must share user-uploaded files between instances. Which storage fits, and why not a block volume attached to one VM?

a.lead: **A network file system** if the app needs **shared file semantics**, or **object storage** if it can use **object APIs**.
items: **Object storage** also lets **web and mobile clients** fetch the files
**Not a block volume**: normally a **disk for one attached VM**, not a **shared filesystem**
**Concurrent writers** on it need **explicit support** and **coordination**

check.q: A team stores its database files on the VM's local instance disk because it is fastest. What is the risk, and what would you change?

items: **Risk**: **instance-store disk** is **ephemeral** → data can disappear on **stop**, **termination** or **host failure**
**Change**: put database files on a **persistent block volume** with suitable **retention** and **backups**, or use a **managed database**
**Local disk**: keep for **scratch data** that can be **regenerated**

check.q: Images must be served to a web app, a mobile app and a partner's batch job. Why is object storage the natural fit?

items: **Object storage** is reached through a **standard web API** → every **channel** and **service model** uses it the same way, **without mounting a disk**
Also the **most flexible** and **widely used** option
a.foot: **Trade-off**: it isn't a **normal filesystem** → apps that expect **file locking** or **in-place edits** need changes.

visuals.title: File storage options
rows: Disks attached to host; IaaS only; data lost if drive fails or instance stops/terminates
Persistent block device; check attachment and deletion settings
Data needing quick access and long-term persistence
Data accessed from many different channels; most flexible

sections.title: AWS storage services and summary
sections.summary: Mapping each persistence option to an AWS managed service, and the wrap-up on polyglot persistence.

items: **EC2 instance store** → **scratch**
**EFS** → **shared files**
**EBS** → **block volumes**
**S3** → **objects**
**RDS/Aurora** → **relational transactions**
**DynamoDB** → **key-value and document** access
**Redshift** → **analytical SQL warehouse**, **not** a NoSQL column-family store
**ElastiCache** → **in-memory caching**
**Neptune** → **graph queries**
**Managed** → **offloads** much **maintenance, backups and availability** work
**Self-host** → when **compatibility, control** or a **missing capability** justifies the **operating burden**
Either way, **still design security, capacity and recovery**
**Unstructured** → **files**
**Structured** → **databases**
**Polyglot persistence** → choosing the **right tool for each use case**

terms.def: AWS managed relational database service supporting several engines.
AWS cloud-built relational database.
AWS managed in-memory cache using Redis or Memcached.
AWS managed graph database.

check.q: A team wants to install a database on a VM instead of using the provider's managed relational database 'to keep control'. When is that justified?

a.lead: **Justified when compatibility**, a needed **extension or version**, or a **capability missing** from the managed option justifies the **operating burden**.
items: **Otherwise managed is the better default**: offloads much **maintenance**, **patching**, **backup** and **availability** work
**Either way**, the customer still designs **access**, **schemas**, **capacity** and **recovery**

check.q: An e-commerce app needs a session cache, a catalogue with varying product attributes, sales analytics and 'customers who bought this also bought' recommendations. Match each to a store type and give the reason.

items: **Session cache** → **in-memory key-value**: **fast keyed access** to **disposable data**
**Catalogue** → **document or key-value**: **attributes vary** per product and items are **read whole**
**Analytics** → **columnar SQL warehouse**: **scans and aggregations**
**Recommendations** → **graph store**: **relationship traversal**
a.foot: Each extra store adds **operational cost** → **drop one** if a **simpler store** meets the need.

exam_angles.q: Design the persistence strategy for a cloud-native e-commerce platform with a catalogue (varying attributes), carts that must survive a cache failure, orders, recommendations and product images. Justify each store and say which one you would drop if the team were only 4 people.

items: **Orders** → **managed relational database**: **ACID transactions**
**Catalogue** → **document store**: **flexible attributes** read as **whole items**
**Carts** → **durable key-value store**, or the relational database, with a **cache in front** → carts must **survive cache loss**
**Recommendations** → **graph store**: **traversal**
**Images** → **object storage** served through a **CDN**

sub: **Drop the graph store** → compute recommendations in **batch** from the **order database**

a.foot: Each extra store adds **programming and operational complexity**.

exam_angles.q: A regional retailer's single relational database can't keep up with growing order writes across Singapore and Malaysia. A teammate proposes read replicas. Evaluate that, then propose how to scale the data tier and name two side effects to monitor.

sub: Won't fix a **write bottleneck** → all writes still go to **one leader**
**Shard orders by country** → each node serves its **own reads and writes**
**Replicate** the **shared, read-heavy product list** to both nodes with **single-leader replication**
Keep **payment data under ACID**; accept **eventual consistency** only where the **business allows**
**Replica lag** on the product list (**stale prices**)

exam_angles.q: Recommend data stores for a global banking ledger and for a social media status feed, and explain why the SQL versus NoSQL label alone doesn't settle the choice.

items: **Ledger** → a **relational or NewSQL store** fits: needs **transactional invariants** and **durability**; weigh **distributed coordination cost** against **scale needs**
**Feed** → a **distributed NoSQL store** with **eventual consistency**: tolerates **briefly stale replicas**, needs high **write and read scale**
a.foot: Decide from **per-operation consistency requirements**, **access patterns** and **coordination cost**.

exam_angles.q: A manager says 'NoSQL replaced relational databases, so all new systems should be NoSQL.' Using the V's of big data and the web-search example, explain why NoSQL emerged and argue whether the claim holds.

items: **Web-search lookup**: needed none of the **joins** or **multi-record transactions** that relational systems provide
**Claim doesn't hold**: relational databases remain the **natural fit** for **constraints**, **joins** and **ACID transactions**
**Polyglot persistence**: use **each model where it fits**
a.foot: Accept the **complexity** only when the **benefit is larger**.

exam_angles.q: An image-processing service has 10 worker VMs. Choose storage for temporary processing scratch space, the job database's data files, configuration shared by all workers, and finished images served to web and mobile apps. Then say what breaks if the shared configuration is put on one VM's block volume.

items: **Scratch** → **ephemeral instance disk**: it can be **regenerated**
**Database files** → **persistent block volume** with **retention** and **backups**, or a **managed database**
**Shared configuration** → **network file system**
**Finished images** → **object storage**, reached through its **API** by both apps

items.t: **Shared config on one VM's block volume**
sub: A block volume is normally **attached to one VM** → the **other 9 workers** couldn't read the configuration
**That VM's failure** would take the configuration with it
